title: "Policy"

This section will look at New York City, USA as a case study city, with their the [OneNYC 2050](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/climate/downloads/pdfs/OneNYC_2050_Strategic_Plan.pdf) strategy's goal to achieve "A Liveable Climate". Like most dense urban areas, New York City (NYC) is also facing the problems of warmer urban temperatures than its rural and suburban neighborhoods. Given growing events of higher frequency, longer lasting and more intense heat waves, this section will focus on one of NYC's experiencing climate threats of [Extreme Heat](https://www.nyc.gov/content/climate/pages/extreme-heat).

## Summary

The OneNYC 2050: Building a Strong and Fair City is a long term strategic plan compromised of 8 goals and 30 initiatives. It aims to achieve an equitable, sustainable and thriving city through addressing its climate change, economic equality, housing, health, education, transportation and infrastructure. Under its "Livable Climate" goal, the strategy sets out the following key initiatives in repsonse to NYC's climate threats. Initiative 21 is directly relevant to the extreme heat challenge, envisioning community level interventions that aims to reduce vulnerability to climate impacts such as rising temperatures.

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| A Livable Climate Initiatives, OneNYC 2050 Strategic Plan                                                        |
+==================================================================================================================+
| 20. Achieve carbon neutrality and 100 percent clean electricity                                                  |
| 21. A LIVABLE CLIMATE Strengthen communities, buildings, infrastructure, and the waterfront to be more resilient |
| 22. Create economic opportunities for all New Yorkers through climate action                                     |
| 23. Fight for climate accountability and justice                                                                 |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

: Relevant Initiatives, Source: [OneNYC 2050](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/climate/downloads/pdfs/OneNYC_2050_Strategic_Plan.pdf)

NYC has identified extreme heat to be one of its major climate threats, where it "is now the number one cause of mortality from weather conditions" ([OneNYC 2050](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/climate/downloads/pdfs/OneNYC_2050_Strategic_Plan.pdf), p.32). Extreme heat within the city also known as the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect, is a challenge that is widely faced by many cities globally. These neighbourhoods tends to have concentrations dark surfaces from built structures, concrete and asphalt that absorbs and retain solar radiation throughout the day, while having limited green space to facilitate natural cooling through evapotranspiration and solar shading. The NYC has also identified limited access to air conditioning, energy costs and poor housing quality as drivers of such heat impacts ([Nyc.gov, 2019](https://www.nyc.gov/content/climate/pages/extreme-heat)).

::: {layout-ncol="1"}
![UHI, Source: [EARTH.ORG](https://earth.org/data_visualization/urban-heat-islands/)](images/w4_images/UHIfig1.jpg)
:::

It is stated that "all heat deaths are preventable" ([Nyc.gov, 2019](https://www.nyc.gov/content/climate/pages/extreme-heat)). The OneNYC uses the Heat Vulnerability Index to identify neighborhoods that are more at risk following extreme heat. The risks are not evenly distributed across the city, where South Bronx, Central Brooklyn and Upper Manhattan are highlighted as the city's most heat vulnerable neighborhoods.

::: {layout-ncol="1"}
![HVI (Data Source: [EJNYC Full Data Explorer](https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/6a3da7b920f248af961554bdf01d668b) )](images/w4_images/NYC_HVI_Map2.png)
:::

In action, the OneNYC strategy is commited to intervene through a range of natural and built solutions, such as promoting urban forests efforts to combat extreme heat, installation of cool roofs to lower local temperatures and mitigate the health impacts from UHI as well as further green infrastructure investments. Next will be looked at how remotely sensed data could be used to address policy goals.

## Application

### Data

Land surface temperature (LST) obtained from satellite sensors are particularly useful for understanding and mapping extreme heat. The Landsat Thematic Mapper (TM)/Enhanced Thematic Mapper (ETM+)/Thermal Infrared Sensor (TIRS) and Terra/Aqua Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) are commonly used for urban heat studies, accounting for around 78% of total publications ([Zhou et. al., 2019](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/11/1/48)). This reflected how widely remotely sensing satellite data has been adopted for research in this field.

However, measuring urban heat also posed several challenges. [Shandas et.al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2225-1154/7/1/5)(2019) discussed two commonly and currently used approaches of ground based temperature and satellite imagery to estimate surface temperatures. Thermal infrared sensors from satellite data record the hotness of physical surfaces, but this will not be the same case of what air temperature humans experiences at street level. For a city where extreme heat can cause deaths, this approach may not be sufficient. Therefore, integrating both methods enables higher accuracy and precision. Such integrated approach has been increasingly seen in heat monitoring tools, including the HVI, which combines land cover from satellite data with ground-level health and social vulnerability indicators.

Similarly, [Mushore et.al., 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/15/23/5461) also suggested the benefits of installing high-resolution thermal comfort mneasuring instruments that are fairly distributed across different parts of an area, capturing experiences to improve remotely sensed data.

## Reflection

Urban greening policies and strategies need to be scaled up at the municipal level to ensure interventions are both comprehensive and economically viable. [Mushore et.al., 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/15/23/5461) study has demonstrated that vegetation and water ecosystems has proven heat mitigation value, alongside the promotion of roof greening as a cost-effective adaptation measure in densely built areas. OneNYC 2050's urban forest and cool roof initiatives operate at precisely this municipal scale, but require sustained investment and coordination across all boroughs to reach the communities most exposed to extreme heat. Without embedding these strategies into long-term planning and funding frameworks, greening efforts may remain a short fall rather than delivering the city-wide temperature reductions solving any urgently need.

Satellite-based thermal infrared (TIR) data, from sensors like Landsat or ASTER, is the most widely used method across studies. However, it captures the temperature on rooftops and pavements surfaces, not the temperature that humans experience at street level. This makes it less of a fit for studies when considering ground level analysis. Therefore, for high precision and accuracy, one solution is to place ground-based measurement "traverses" models in different areas across the city. This enables observations of variation of temperature across different land uses and land covers, providing a more throughout assessment of urban heat across the city. Critically, this method is more expensive and resource intensive for a placement coverage across an entire city.

In NYC, while Landsat/MODIS LST data effectively supports city-wide Heat Vulnerability Index mapping, yet its inability to capture ground-level human-experienced temperatures remains a methodological limitation that should be considered for urban heat mitigation.

Overall, remotely sensed data remains significant potential in monitoring and understanding urban heat. It offers a more direct and accurate observation to understand the development of our cities, which is critical for informing policy decision-makings.
